item: Basis of the claim: Law 90-11 on labour relations, the worker's right to a regular wage for work done (wage articles, payment at each due date, components of the wage, overtime, bonuses and allowances), read with the employment contract and any collective agreement.
Element 1: an employment relationship with the defendant (written or unwritten contract; Law 90-11 allows proof of the relationship by any means), its start date, the post and the agreed wage.
Element 2: work actually performed (or time at the employer's disposal) for the period claimed; wages are the counterpart of work, so periods of unpaid absence are excluded.
Element 3: non-payment by the employer of the sums claimed (base wage, overtime, bonuses, allowances), with the period and the amount of each item.

Burden of proof: the worker proves the relationship and the work; the employer, as debtor, proves payment (civil code rule that the creditor proves the obligation and the debtor proves release); payslips and the payroll register are the employer's documents.
Payslip: the employer must deliver a payslip with each payment; ask whether payslips exist and what they show; a signed payslip without reservation may be argued as proof of payment.
Overtime: check it was ordered or accepted by the employer, the legal limits, and the rate of increase set by Law 90-11 and the collective agreement.

Prior step: mandatory conciliation before the labour inspectorate's conciliation office (Law 90-04 on individual labour disputes) before any claim to the social section; the petition must attach the record of non-conciliation.
Before conciliation: the internal procedure inside the employer (collective agreement procedure or referral to the superior and management) under Law 90-04; check whether it was used.

Exceptions to conciliation: Law 90-04 lists cases where conciliation is not required (for example the employer residing abroad, or the employer in judicial settlement or bankruptcy); check which apply.

Partial conciliation: if a conciliation record settled part of the dispute, that part is enforced by the president of the social section (enforcement order), not claimed anew; only the remainder is sued on.

Time limit to file after non-conciliation: CPCM provides that the claim is filed within six months of the delivery of the record of non-conciliation, on pain of forfeiture; check the delivery date, count the six months, and whether the forfeiture is raised by the court.

Limitation of wage claims: the civil code sets a short limitation for workers' wages (I recall one year for wages of workers and servants, with the creditor's oath available to the debtor), and a five-year limitation for periodic renewable rights; to be confirmed in the text.
Start of limitation: each wage instalment prescribes from its own due date; check the oldest unpaid month.
Interruption of limitation: by a judicial claim, an acknowledgement by the debtor; check whether referral to the conciliation office interrupts limitation (Law 90-04 or the civil code).
Limitation is not raised by the court of its own motion; only on the defendant's plea.
Competent section: the social section of the tribunal (CPCM articles on the social section: individual labour disputes, wages, contracts of employment, training and apprenticeship).
Composition: the social section sits with assessors (workers' and employers' representatives); check that the court has a social section, otherwise the rules on courts without sections apply.

Territorial jurisdiction: CPCM social matters: the court of the place where the contract was concluded or performed, or the plaintiff's domicile in specific cases (contract suspended or terminated by work accident or occupational disease); check whether this rule is of public order.

Exit: civil servants and contractual agents of public administrative institutions governed by the general civil service statute (Ordinance 06-03) go before the administrative court, not the social section.

Exit: a claim based on a criminal offence (for example the employer's criminal liability for non-payment) may be brought before the criminal judge as a civil party; check for a pending criminal case on the same facts.
Exit: an order to pay (CPCM) might be considered for a fixed written debt, but the labour conciliation rule and social section specificity apply; check whether an order to pay was already issued.
Accessory request: damages for delay in payment (civil code: damages for delay require a formal notice, except listed cases; interest between individuals prohibited); check the formal notice.

Accessory request: provisional execution: Law 90-04 gives provisional execution by right to judgments on payment of wages and allowances for the last six months; CPCM provisional execution rules for the rest.
Judgment in first and last resort: Law 90-04 lists matters judged without appeal (for example issuing payslips or work certificates); wage claims generally are subject to appeal.
Wage preference: wages are a privileged debt ranking before other creditors (Law 90-11 and civil code privilege); relevant if the employer is insolvent or in bankruptcy.
Employer in bankruptcy or judicial settlement: the claim must be declared in the collective procedure; check the specialised commercial court and the suspension of individual actions.
Minimum wage (SNMG): if the agreed wage is below the national guaranteed minimum wage, the difference may be claimed; check the applicable decree.
Documents: record of non-conciliation, employment contract or proof of relationship, payslips, social-security affiliation, statement of sums claimed month by month, formal notice if any.
Petition formal elements: CPCM mandatory elements of the petition, identity of the employer (natural or legal person, its representative), fees.

Boundaries: dismissal compensation, abusive dismissal damages, end-of-service or redundancy compensation, and social-security benefits (social security disputes go to the social section under a different procedure with prior internal appeal) are distinct claims.
Boundary: wages of a domestic worker or a contract that is in truth a service or agency contract (civil code) rather than employment; check subordination.

Amendments: Law 90-04 amended in 1991; Law 90-11 amended several times (1991, 1996 ordinance, 1997 ordinance); CPCM Law 08-09 amended by Law 22-13 (specialised commercial courts); check current versions.
Is the plaintiff an employee bound to the defendant by an employment relationship (written or not), and is the defendant the employer?
What is the exact nature of each sum claimed: wage, bonus, allowance, overtime, paid leave, end-of-service entitlements?
What is the amount owed for each period, and what proof exists (contract, payslips, attendance, witnesses)?
Has the employee exhausted the internal procedure of the employer (collective agreement, hierarchy) where it applies?
Was the matter brought before the conciliation office of the labour inspectorate, and was a record of non-conciliation delivered?
Is there a record of conciliation (agreement on part of the dispute) that limits what may still be claimed?
By what date must the claim be filed after the record of non-conciliation, and what is the sanction for filing late?
Is the claim filed before the social section of the court, and what if the court has no such section?
Which court has territorial jurisdiction: place of the work, place of the contract, or the employer's seat?
Is the dispute one for the ordinary courts, or does it escape them (public employer under statute, administrative decision)?
Is the employer a public administrative body, so that the administrative judge may be the one to hear it?
What limitation period applies to wages and related claims, from what date does it run, and how is it counted?
Does the limitation run during the employment relationship, and what interrupts or suspends it?
Who may raise limitation, and may the court raise it of its own motion?
Is a formal notice required before claiming damages for delay, and in what form?
Are damages for late payment claimable, on what conditions, and with what proof of harm?
Is interest or a penalty payment claimable on wages, and from what date?
May provisional execution be requested for wages, and on what conditions?
Is the employee exempt from court fees for this claim?
What must the petition contain: court, parties, facts, claims, and the documents attached?
Who bears the burden of proving the relationship, the work done, and the payment of wages?
May the employee prove the relationship and the wages by all means, or is writing required?
Is the employer required to keep pay records, and may their absence be used against him?
Are the claimed wages protected against deduction or set-off, and what part may the employer withhold?
Does a payment or a receipt signed by the employee settle the claim, and what is its force?
Does the claim also involve a dismissal or termination that should be pleaded separately?
Is a request for a certificate of work or a pay statement to be added as an accessory request?
Are the costs and lawyer fees claimable, and under which text?
Is a lawyer mandatory in this court for this kind of claim?
Does the plaintiff have the status to sue (capacity, standing), and is a representative such as a union able to act?
